clue.text: Mum looks quite different

indicators.note: the word quite is made different, its letters put into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone's mother is looking unlike her usual self.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mum' looks like a mother, but it is the adjective meaning silent; 'different' rearranges QUITE.
explanation.definitionFit: Keeping mum means saying nothing, so mum is a synonym for silent.

clue.text: But it's not fives that they play

definitions.text: But it's not fives that they play

parts.words: But it's not fives that they play
parts.note: fives is a ball game played with the hand; a group of five musicians plays music, not that game

explanation.surface: A team who are not fives players.
explanation.walkthrough: FIVES is a British handball game; a group of five players performs music as a five, not the game of fives.
explanation.definitionFit: A quintette is a group of five musicians who play together.

clue.text: I strike a blow for the faith

parts.note: to slam is to hit or bang hard

explanation.surface: Someone declaring they are fighting for their religion.
explanation.definitionFit: The religion of Muslims, one of the world's great faiths.

clue.text: A pair of braces

parts.note: a brace is a pair, so two braces are two pairs, counted as a sum

explanation.surface: Two sets of trouser suspenders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Braces' suggests trouser suspenders, but a brace (of pheasants, say) is simply two, so two of them is two lots of two.
explanation.definitionFit: Two pairs side by side make a pair plus a pair, the sum of four in a children's sum.

clue.text: Theatrical accommodation for ponies in a mine ?

explanation.surface: Somewhere for pit ponies to be housed in a mine.
explanation.walkthrough: PIT ponies hauled coal in British mines; the pit stalls were the old cheap seats behind the stalls in a theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatre seats at the back of the ground floor, and stabling compartments below ground for working ponies.

clue.text: Not where the mad stop in Germany — just the' reverse

indicators.note: the clue tells us to take the words mad and stop and read the pair backwards

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A place in Germany that is not where lunatics halt, but the opposite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not where the' is surface padding: the clue pretends to name a halt for lunatics, then says to read the phrase the other way to reach the German city.
explanation.definitionFit: Potsdam is a city in Germany, near Berlin, site of the 1945 conference.

clue.text: Where to get rain, possibly in Africa

definitions.note: the definition is a place in Africa, introduced by Where

indicators.note: the letters of get rain possibly form something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: A traveller wondering where in Africa one might find rain.
explanation.definitionFit: Tangier is a Moroccan port city on the north coast of Africa.

clue.text: See to it — it has reached boiling-point

definitions.text: See to it — it has reached boiling-point

parts.words: See to it — it has reached boiling-point
parts.note: put SEE in front of the word meaning 'it' and the result means boiling or furious

explanation.surface: An instruction to deal with a pan that has come to the boil.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'See to it' literally: add SEE to the answer (a word for 'it') and you get SEETHING, which has reached boiling-point.
explanation.definitionFit: An object or entity, any 'it', is called a thing.

clue.text: Greenwich has ' none to speak of

definitions.text: Greenwich has ' none to speak of

parts.words: Greenwich has ' none to speak of
parts.note: the prime meridian runs through Greenwich, so its east-west position is zero degrees

explanation.surface: A remark that a London borough has very little of something.
explanation.walkthrough: GREENWICH, in London, defines the prime meridian, so its east-west angular position is nil.
explanation.definitionFit: The east-west angular position of a place, measured in degrees from the meridian.

clue.text: Scene of Berliners' aquatic frolics ?

parts.note: the river through Berlin, where locals swim, shares its name with a word for a bout of frolicking

explanation.surface: Where Berlin folk go to play in the water.
explanation.walkthrough: The Spree is the river through Berlin, and a spree is also a bout of frolics.
explanation.definitionFit: Berlin's river, and also a lively bout of indulgence or fun.

clue.text: It surely doesn't describe the, doctor's gains ?

definitions.text: It surely doesn't describe the, doctor's gains ?

parts.words: It surely doesn't describe the, doctor's gains ?
parts.note: a doctor earns from those who are unwell, so the fees are 'got' from the sick, yet they are honest

explanation.surface: A protest that a physician's earnings are not dishonest.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the word: a doctor's money is gotten from the ill, yet it is not dishonestly acquired.
explanation.definitionFit: Ill-gotten means obtained dishonestly or unfairly.

clue.text: This man needs food, including bull !

explanation.surface: A hungry man who wants a meal, beef and all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The inner man' is the stomach or appetite; on a target, the inner is the ring round the bull's-eye.
explanation.definitionFit: The appetite (the inner man craves food), and the target ring next to and including the bull's-eye.

clue.text: I'm not prepared for a Shakespearian role

indicators.note: the letters of I'm not are prepared, worked up into a new form

explanation.surface: An actor confessing they have not learnt their Shakespeare part.
explanation.definitionFit: Timon of Athens is the title character of a Shakespeare play.

clue.text: Those who are have their own convictions

definitions.text: Those who are have their own convictions

parts.words: Those who are have their own convictions
parts.note: convictions here are court sentences, not firm beliefs: people serving a prison term

explanation.surface: Praise for people who hold firm beliefs of their own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Convictions' suggests opinions, but means criminal convictions: prisoners are serving sentences.
explanation.definitionFit: Serving a prison sentence is called doing time.

clue.text: Dickensian who invoked a general blessing

definitions.text: Dickensian who invoked a general blessing

parts.words: Dickensian who invoked a general blessing
parts.note: the sickly Cratchit boy in A Christmas Carol says 'God bless us, every one'

explanation.surface: A Dickens character who called down a blessing on all.
explanation.walkthrough: In A Christmas Carol the crippled Cratchit child's famous line is 'God bless us, every one!'
explanation.definitionFit: The youngest Cratchit son, a character in Dickens's A Christmas Carol.

clue.text: But not necessarily unsound

parts.note: unsound read literally is without sound, which is not the same as faulty

explanation.surface: A cautious remark that something is not necessarily faulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unsound' normally means faulty; read as 'without sound' it describes something silent.
explanation.definitionFit: Making no sound at all; silent.

clue.text: Obliged once, more to make a comeback ?

parts.note: re- is the prefix meaning again, once more
bound means obliged, as in duty-bound

explanation.surface: Someone forced yet again to stage a return.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma after 'once' is a newspaper misprint; 'once more' gives RE.
explanation.definitionFit: To rebound is to spring back, as a ball does after hitting a wall.

clue.text: A Gilbertian kingdom

parts.note: the realm in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Gondoliers

explanation.surface: A make-believe realm from comic opera.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Gondoliers by Gilbert and Sullivan, the two gondoliers jointly reign over this island kingdom.
explanation.definitionFit: The imaginary island realm ruled jointly in The Gondoliers.

clue.text: Underworld area of operations of an anatomist

parts.note: Dis is the Roman god of the underworld and his realm
a sector is a military zone of operations

explanation.surface: The patch of a criminal gang where an anatomist works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Underworld' suggests crime, but it is DIS, the classical realm of the dead.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who cuts up bodies to study their structure, as an anatomist does.

clue.text: Pressmen become tired so easily

indicators.note: the letters of tired so are rearranged easily, i.e. freely

explanation.surface: Journalists wearing out quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: Newspaper staff who prepare copy, journalists of the press.

clue.text: Seven members of the Cliff family

definitions.text: Seven members of the Cliff family

parts.words: Seven members of the Cliff family
parts.note: a famous chain of chalk cliffs on the Sussex coast is named as seven female siblings

explanation.surface: Seven relatives from a family surnamed Cliff.
explanation.walkthrough: The Seven Sisters are chalk cliffs on the English coast of Sussex; 'Cliff' poses as a surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Female siblings, here the seven chalk cliffs counted as one family.

clue.text: Do these artisans find difficulty in going straight ?

definitions.text: Do these artisans find difficulty in going straight ?

parts.words: Do these artisans find difficulty in going straight ?
parts.note: going straight hints at reformed criminals, but these craftsmen work on a lathe, always rotating

explanation.surface: Wondering whether craftsmen struggle to give up crime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going straight' suggests reformed criminals; these lathe workers spend their days turning wood or metal round.
explanation.definitionFit: People who shape wood or metal on a lathe.

clue.text: Wordsworth composed upstream from this abbey

definitions.text: Wordsworth composed upstream from this abbey

parts.words: Wordsworth composed upstream from this abbey
parts.note: the poem 'Lines Composed a Few Miles above' a ruined Wye valley abbey

explanation.surface: A note that the poet wrote some lines a little upriver of an abbey.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth's poem title is 'Lines Composed a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey', on the River Wye in Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruined Cistercian abbey in the Wye valley, Monmouthshire.

clue.text: Unrestrained author is a member of a fraternity

parts.note: free means not restrained
A. E. W. Mason was the author of The Four Feathers

explanation.surface: An uninhibited writer who belongs to a brotherhood.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the secret brotherhood of Freemasons.

clue.text: There will be great excitement if ever I leave !

indicators.note: the letter I is to leave, departing from the words if ever

explanation.surface: Someone warning that their departure would cause a stir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leave' removes the I from IF EVER.
explanation.definitionFit: A fever is a state of intense nervous excitement, as in a fever pitch.

clue.text: Prodigal announcing identity of this particle

definitions.text: Prodigal announcing identity of this particle

parts.words: Prodigal announcing identity of this particle
parts.note: the returning prodigal son, saying who he is, cries '...', which sounds like the particle's name

explanation.surface: A wasteful man revealing what a tiny particle is.
explanation.walkthrough: The prodigal son announcing himself might say 'Me, son!', which sounds like the name of a subatomic particle.
explanation.definitionFit: A meson is a subatomic particle made of a quark and an antiquark.

clue.text: The right name

explanation.surface: Insisting on the correct word.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal right of ownership, as in title to land, and the name of a book or work.

clue.text: What this rope-walker should not be

definitions.text: What this rope-walker should not be

parts.words: What this rope-walker should not be
parts.note: the walker on a taut rope must not be drunk; the slang word for drunk also describes the rope

explanation.surface: Advice about what a circus performer must avoid.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 'tightrope-walker': the rope is taut, but the walker must not be drunk, which is also called tight.
explanation.definitionFit: Tight is slang for drunk.

clue.text: Prospects for wives, perhaps

indicators.note: the letters of wives perhaps make another word when rearranged

explanation.surface: Considering how good the outlook is for married women.
explanation.definitionFit: Views are vistas or outlooks, i.e. prospects.

clue.text: Is the soldier a sight better for this order ?

definitions.text: Is the soldier a sight better for this order ?

parts.words: Is the soldier a sight better for this order ?
parts.note: a parade-ground command makes soldiers turn their heads, and 'a sight better' hints at improved vision

explanation.surface: Asking whether a soldier looks better after being given a command.
explanation.walkthrough: The drill command turns heads to the right; 'a sight better' plays on eyes being put right.
explanation.definitionFit: A parade-ground command to turn the head to the right in salute.

clue.text: It 'is only to be seen in the Far East

definitions.text: It 'is only to be seen in the Far East

parts.words: It 'is only to be seen in the Far East
parts.note: the dawn sun appears only in the eastern sky, and the Far East's Japan uses it as an emblem

explanation.surface: Something visible only in East Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: The morning sun is seen only in the east, and Japan is the Land of the Rising Sun.
explanation.definitionFit: The sun at dawn, rising in the east, and Japan's emblem.

clue.text: He. plays when he works in a factory

indicators.note: the word sits inside the letters of a factory, a run within

explanation.surface: A man who performs while employed in a factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'works in' reads like employment, but the performer is inside the letters of 'a factory'.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor performs in plays.
